source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

In the bustling aisle, the conveyor belt hummed steadily, the barcodes scanned one after another with precise clicks. Amidst the items, a cart loomed large, filled to the brim; a divider bar stood between it and the next customer eagerly waiting. Behind them, a shopper was jostled by another impatient soul, their bags nudging the partition slightly. The cashier's screen flickered softly, each beep marking an item’s journey through the line.

Before the receipt printer sprang to life with a familiar hiss, the total appeared: $24.50. A loyalty-card prompt flashed invitingly on the register. The shopper took out their card, swiping it confidently as the machine hummed confirmation. Meanwhile, the bagger gathered items from the conveyor and placed them in a plastic tote, stacking them neatly.

The friction between the divider bar and the cart grew palpable; the cashier shifted slightly to accommodate the new pressure. The line continued its steady flow, each transaction blending into a familiar rhythm. Yet beneath the surface, subtle tensions simmered as the queue tested the boundaries of space.

At the bustling hour, a cart edged along the conveyor belt, its contents scanned by a glowing scanner. A shopper placed items there, their hands moving briskly through the bagging area. Behind stood another, eagerly waiting to claim space in line.

The cashier’s screen flickered with beeps, each one a crisp reminder of retail process; totals were announced with cold precision. Loyalty-card prompts flashed softly, but neither paused for such distractions.

In the narrow aisle, a divider bar stood as silent sentinel, between the two impatient figures. A receipt was prepared, slid over the card reader at the register's call.

Annoyance flickered as both shoppers edged closer, the air thick with tension. Small, almost unnoticeable friction over queue position ensued, a whisper of conflict in the smooth flow of the line.

Beneath the fluorescent lights, routine hummed—beeps echoing, total announced, card read once more. The cashier’s eyes flicked to each shopper in turn, efficient yet somewhat strained by the unexpected delay.

Items swirled around the belt, scanned swiftly, bagged and placed at the edge of the counter. The second shopper began to move forward, a challenge in their stance, but no one budged from the pre-ordained order.

The register stood as an immutable marker, its machine-like efficiency unyielding. Beeps repeated, numbers tallied, finality sealing the retail transaction.

In the confined space of the queue, tension simmered just beneath the surface—annoyance and a barely restrained desire for faster service. Yet, each person remained in their appointed place, the conveyor belt undeterred by human frailty.

In the rush hour queue, the conveyor belt hummed with movement, and a shopper's cart slid past the barcode scanner. Behind them, another shopper jostled for space, the divider bar a thin barrier between their baskets. The cashier greeted with a wave of the card reader as the total beeps across the air. 

On the screen appeared the amount due, a reminder to swipe the loyalty card. The shopper's eyes flicked over the items, their fingers reaching out to touch. Nearby, the previous customer’s receipt crinkled slightly in the bin. 

In the background, the friction of another body pressed into the line. The cashier paused for a moment, a small frown on her face as she considered the space shortage. "Just one more item," she spoke softly, adjusting the divider.

The new shopper nodded, pulling an extra bag from their cart. The conveyor belt resumed its steady rhythm, and the beeps of items being scanned continued. Behind them, the crowd began to shift, others waiting for their turn. 

A moment passed with the card reader beeping again, the total on screen clear as day. The shopper took a deep breath, deciding on the loyalty-card prompt. "Sure," they said, swiping the card swiftly.

The register beeped one final time, and the receipt printer whirred to life. As the bagging area began its task, the line flowed forward again, another transaction completed in the retail routine of busy hours.

In the bustling queue, shoppers moved like grains of sand on a conveyor belt. The scanner's hum seemed to vibrate through the air as it read each item. Beyond lay the tidy dividers and bagging station; to the side, a card reader awaited.

Another shopper pushed forward, almost spilling the contents of their cart over the divider. Frustration crackled in the thinning space between them. The cashier's fingers danced across the keyboard, beeps echoing softly with each item scanned.

The register announced totals clearly, prompting loyalty-card queries. A receipt slipped out, its edges curling slightly as it was pressed into the shopper’s palm.

Past those moments of tension, the same routine played out: beep, beep, announce total, prompt card, hand over receipt. Each cycle smooth but for the occasional friction between customers, a reminder that time, like money in this line, was moving inexorably forward.

In the hustle at the end of the aisle, a cart laden with essentials nudged against the divider, its contents clearly visible. Behind loomed another shopper, whose cart's edge almost crossed over, sparking a momentary pause. The conveyor belt hummed steadily, items gliding by like silent passengers on their journey to bagging and beyond.

Beside them, a cashier tapped keys on the register, her eyes scanning barcodes and adding up the tally with practiced speed. A receipt printer whirred quietly into life, the paper snaking out in neat increments. The loyalty-card slot above beckoned, promising points and deals but holding off today as neither customer reached for it.

A small argument arose over the flow of the queue, both customers shifting slightly to make way without too much fuss, each trying not to obstruct the next in line. The beep of the scanner was constant, a monotonous yet necessary tune marking each item's progress toward totalling.

The total appeared on the screen: $13.25. "Would you like your usual?" the cashier asked, her voice clear and steady over the hubbub. Another nod from the first customer as the second lingered at the edge of the transaction, clearly weighing their options before finally stepping forward to pay.

In the humming line, behind the divider bar and the scanner's glowing, there moved a trolley filled with groceries. A bagging area stood next to the cashier, who tapped her fingers on the register, waiting. The conveyor belt buzzed under the beeps of scanned items.

Behind us, another shopper shuffled close, causing the cart to brush gently against mine. "Sorry," she muttered, peering over the divider at the impatient queue forming behind me.

The register's hum turned to a quickened tone as each item was announced. The total flashed on a small screen: $35.75. A loyalty card prompt flickered softly, promising points and discounts.

"Can you speed up?" she asked, her eyes darting nervously back towards the tail of the line.

The cashier's response was brisk but calm: "Just a moment." She swiped my loyalty card, linking it to the purchase. The beeps softened as the machine registered the transaction.

A small friction arose when another customer pushed their cart closer, nearly bumping into mine. I glanced over, feeling the urge to complain, but held back. We were all in this together, after all.

The line moved steadily on, the conveyor belt's rhythm punctuated by the sharp clicks of the scanner. Each item was added with precise efficiency as if following a routine so familiar it felt almost mechanical.

Behind me, someone cleared their throat, bringing the momentary silence to an end: "Could you...?"

"Just let me finish here," she replied gently, her voice steady despite the growing impatience around us.

The register's final beep signified the completion of my transaction. The receipt slipped out, crisp and clean in my hand. I stepped forward, feeling a mix of relief and anticipation as the next line shuffled into place.
